Audi 5000
OW-dee FIVE THOU-zund
interjection, phrase (Gen X slang)
A pun from late-1980s hip-hop and street speech: Audi sounds like "outta" (as in "I’m outta here"), and the Audi 5000 was the German luxury sedan sold in America through the 1980s. "I’m Audi 5000" or simply "Audi 5000!" meant "I’m leaving, goodbye"; it merged in the early 1990s with outtie to give I’m outtie 5000. The car brand itself takes its name from the Latin audi, "listen!" — a Latin rendering of its founder August Horch’s surname (German horch, hark).

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"I’m Audi 5000" is a Gen X goodbye with a grin: "Class is over — I’m Audi." The joke is a sound-alike: Audi for "outta," and the sleek 1980s sedan for the speed of the exit. It is a harmless phrase, and a father has no reason to scold it. But every goodbye is a small rehearsal for the larger ones, and Scripture is wise about departures. "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven" (Ecc 3:1) — a time to arrive and a time to go. The believer’s comings and goings are watched over: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore" (Psa 121:8). Our Lord used His own departure to comfort His disciples: "I go to prepare a place for you" (Joh 14:2). And Paul faced the last goodbye with something close to eagerness: "having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Php 1:23); "the time of my departure is at hand" (2Ti 4:6). That is the Christian’s final I’m outta here — not an escape but a homecoming. A father can use the slang at the door and the theology at the bedside: leave a room well, say goodbye kindly, and live so that when your last departure comes you can say with Paul that you have finished your course and kept the faith.

Webster 1828 Definition

Late-1980s hip-hop pun (Audi = "outta," after the 1980s Audi 5000 sedan) for "I’m leaving"; Scripture watches over every going out (Psa 121:8) and calls the believer’s last departure far better (Php 1:23).

AUDI 5000, interj. (Gen X slang, late 1980s–1990s, hip-hop and street speech) I’m leaving; goodbye; I’m out of here. "Bell just rang — I’m Audi 5000."

Shortened to Audi; blended with outtie as I’m outtie 5000. A sound-alike pun on "outta" and the 1980s Audi 5000 sedan.

Companions: I’m out, let’s jet, peace out, later.

No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is a late-20th-century American pun on a car model.

Decode for parents: "Audi 5000" just means goodbye; use it to teach that the LORD keeps our going out and coming in (Psa 121:8).

Key Scripture

Ecc 3:1 — "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:"

Psa 121:8 — "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore."

Joh 14:2 — "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you."

Php 1:23 — "For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:"

2Ti 4:6 — "For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand."

Modern Corruption

Audi 5000 is a harmless goodbye; its only shadow is a culture of quick exits that never learns to leave well — Scripture keeps every going out under God’s eye and makes the last departure a homecoming.

expand to see more

The quick exit. The phrase celebrates speed: gone before anyone can ask a question. Most of the time that is just fun. But a generation that perfected the quick exit also perfected the unanswered call, the dropped friendship, and the marriage walked out of without a word. Scripture teaches that there is a time to depart (Ecc 3:1), and it implies there is a way: with honesty, with thanks, and with the bridges left standing. The LORD who preserves our going out (Psa 121:8) cares how we go.

The last goodbye. Every I’m outta here is a small picture of the final one. For the unbeliever it is the darkest word in the language; for the Christian it is a door. Christ went ahead to prepare a place (Joh 14:2), and Paul could call his departure "far better" (Php 1:23). A child who learns that early will say goodbye at the door more lightly, and at the graveside with hope.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin audi (listen!) → Audi motor company → the 1980s Audi 5000 sedan → hip-hop pun I’m Audi 5000 ("I’m outta here") → outtie 5000; Scripture: a desire to depart, and to be with Christ (Php 1:23).
